title: Whom do you seek? (John 18:1–11)
hook: soldiers with torches; he steps forward: I am he, and they fall back

segments.voice: Yesterday, the prayer widened to everyone who would ever believe. Your line was that they may be one. What generous thing did you say? Day six hundred forty-two.

The prayer is over. They walk out into the dark, across the brook Kidron, into a garden on the other side. John says Judas knew the place, because Jesus often went there with his friends. And Judas comes. With him, a band of soldiers and officers from the chief priests and Pharisees, carrying lanterns and torches and weapons. A quiet garden at night, and suddenly a line of firelight moving through it. And Jesus doesn't wait to be found.

John tells it this way, in the King James Bible: Jesus, "knowing all things that should come upon him, went forth, and said unto them, Whom seek ye?" He steps forward. They answer, Jesus of Nazareth. And he says two words: I am he. Then something strange happens. "As soon then as he had said unto them, I am he, they went backward, and fell to the ground." Why would armed men fall over? Look at the Greek. What he says is ego eimi, I am. The he is added in English to make the sentence smooth; many printings of the King James put it in italics to show it isn't in the Greek. And all through John's Gospel, I am has been doing heavy lifting. I am the bread of life. I am the light of the world. Before Abraham was, I am. Some readers hear in it an echo of God's name given to Moses at the burning bush, I AM. So when the soldiers stagger back, John seems to be showing who is really in charge in this garden. Not the soldiers. Then Jesus asks again, and this time he bargains, not for himself, but for his friends: if you're looking for me, let these go their way. Peter has other ideas. He pulls a sword and cuts off the right ear of the high priest's servant. Only John gives us the servant's name: Malchus. And Jesus says: "Put up thy sword into the sheath: the cup which my Father hath given me, shall I not drink it?" No fighting. He walks into it with his eyes open.

then, large: `SHALL I NOT DRINK IT?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: step forward in one hard moment. Settle, and breathe. Think of something hard that's coming toward you. A conversation you're dreading, a bill, a diagnosis, an apology you owe. Notice the urge to hide in the trees until it finds you. Now picture yourself stepping forward first, calm, and saying, in your own way, here I am. Breathe there. If you pray, you can ask for that kind of courage. If you don't, simply rehearse the first step. The bell holds the time.
Whom do you seek? Jesus's question to the soldiers in the garden, asked as he steps forward to meet them, not waiting to be found.
Your line: I am he. Today, take the first step toward the hard thing you pictured, before it comes looking for you. Day six hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Many churches read John's account of the arrest during Holy Week, and on Good Friday in a number of traditions the whole Passion according to John is read or sung aloud, often with different readers taking the parts.

original.note: Greek: I am. the words behind 'I am he', and behind John's 'I am' sayings.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus is identifying himself to the soldiers.
what it means: he steps forward, and two words knock armed men to the ground. he's the one in charge in this garden.
what a scholar hears: ego eimi, the same 'I am' as 8:58, which many readers connect with God's name at the burning bush (Exodus 3:14).

notes: KJV prints 'he' in italics in 'I am he' (18:5, 6, 8) to mark a supplied word. Confirm.
Connection of ego eimi with Exodus 3:14 is a common reading, presented as 'many readers hear'. Confirm.
The arresting party: 'a band of men and officers from the chief priests and Pharisees' (18:3). Script says 'soldiers and officers from the chief priests'; check fairness and accuracy.
Only John names Malchus and Peter (18:10). Confirm.
